html:
This comes from my answer to another question, comparing life in Germany and the Netherlands:

“Do you regret studying in the Netherlands?” – Fanyu Meng’s answer – Zhihu

https://www.zhihu.com/question/39192921/answer/334448008


==============================================

Four years living in Germany, five months so far in the Netherlands. On balance: liking it > regretting it. Or, to be precise, no regrets at all. Since I haven’t lived anywhere else for long, I can only compare these two countries:

1. People and culture
Germans have a reputation for being cold and serious. Individuals vary, of course, but most foreigners in Germany find it hard to fit in; Germans are not easy to get close to. The Netherlands is different. The Dutch are on the whole more open and outgoing, keener to really get to know you, and great at jokes, sometimes with no f***ing filter whatsoever. Language is naturally a big part of it. Germany is a big country that takes its language very seriously and protects it on every front. You can survive without a word of German, but it will trip you up at every turn. Everything about the place sends your motivation through the roof: everyone ends up saying danke and bitte. Don’t expect the young guys and girls or the uncles and aunties at the supermarket, whatever their skin color, to speak English to you. Quite possibly they can; they just won’t.

Now the Netherlands. After five months of working here, all I can say is dank u wel, tot ziens and alstublieft (quite possibly misspelled). Oh, and het volgende station, which I picked up from the train announcements. If memory serves, I’ve used them fewer than ten times in total. Shameful, really. Still, thanks to the mighty German language, knowing German helps a lot with Dutch: I can read plenty of sentences. Listening and speaking are a lost cause, though. In the Netherlands hardly anyone can’t speak English, from the lady at the supermarket to construction workers. I later learned that the Netherlands has ranked first in English proficiency among non-native-speaking countries year after year. The other striking difference is that the Dutch are happy to speak English, and together with their personality, that gives the place a very open, big-hearted feel.

Here’s a joke a Dutch person told me (it may also be true). Anyone who has lived in the border region between the two countries will know that German is the lingua franca there. The reason: the Germans think everyone wants to learn German, so they’re helping the Dutch practice; the Dutch think speaking German makes the Germans happy, so they speak German. Everyone is happy. Win-win.

Another reason the Dutch speak such good English is that imported English-language TV (and they watch a lot of American and British TV) is shown in the original, with Dutch subtitles, much as in many Scandinavian countries. Germany, like our own “Amazing China” (to borrow the title of a patriotic Chinese documentary), dubs everything.

Oh, and one more thing. The Netherlands has few people, and you get the feeling it needs foreigners to help build the country. Just look at the students of every color, from Asia, Africa, Latin America and everywhere else, who fill the Dutch technical universities. Germany, meanwhile, is a vast nation of more than 80 million people (roughly, pardon me, the number of P*rty members in our Celestial Empire). German universities still mainly serve German students, foreigners on the academic staff are rarer still, and staying on at a German university is hard.

2. Pay
Obviously Germany is better by who knows how far! A PhD student can take home over €2,000 after tax; a friend of mine who went to work at Mercedes-Benz after his master’s takes home close to €3,000. And the cost of living is low! In Germany, €30 at the supermarket bought a whole pile of stuff; since coming to the Netherlands I get through €50 without even trying. Rents in the Netherlands are ridiculously high too: a room in student housing is basically €600 and up. Germany, by comparison, is dirt cheap. Take Aachen, where I lived: the cheapest student dorm room was just €175, with water, electricity and heating included! Even in Munich, student housing is only €200–300.

Here in the Netherlands, a colleague’s husband works in construction and takes home €1,900 after tax, which floored me. Engineering companies may pay a bit more; I’ve heard of people at ASML (a mechatronics company) making €3,000, but I haven’t checked.

3. Food
This one calls for a proper rant. I used to believe German food was the worst in the world, bar none. Friends told me Britain was worse still, but I stood by my verdict. Then I came to the Netherlands... What the university cafeteria serves can barely be called food, and it is absurdly expensive. When I first arrived, innocent and naive, I wasn’t very hungry one day and thought I’d just grab a little something. At the till: €8.80. I wanted to smash the tray, but my hand, as if of its own accord, met the cashier’s smile and pressed my card to the reader.

Exhibit A: a portion of mashed potato, a meat stick and a bowl of swill that calls itself soup.

The one below looks decent enough, but may I point out that the meat sauce in the middle is the same stuff as the next day’s (or the previous day’s) Bolognese? -_-

Apart from a pitiful handful of hot dishes, it’s basically bread, sandwiches, salads and the like. I’m honestly not a picky eater, and I don’t insist on Chinese food, but every lunchtime I miss the Sauerbraten and Schnitzel of the German cafeterias terribly. In Germany I rarely brought lunch from home; I thought food reheated in the microwave tasted bad. Now, whenever I can cook, I bring my own without fail, and eating it is pure bliss.


4. Work (research)
Maybe my old institute in Germany was just unusually freestyle, but here everyone seems to work so hard! At seven on a Friday evening there are still people on our floor. In Germany, Friday was essentially an arbeitsfrei, work-free, day, which is surely how Freitag got its name. 10:00 group meeting. 11:00 colloquium. 12:00 Friday prayers, i.e. lunch at a restaurant in town. Back for coffee in the kitchen, back at your desk by 13:30–14:00, maybe another coffee break at 15:00, beer o’clock at 16:00, and then schönes Wochenende: have a nice weekend.

I’ve heard similar stories from other institutes. One thing is certain, though: German doctoral training is free-range. My German colleagues back then had one meeting a year with the professor, and even then they didn’t seem to talk about research... Every PhD student is a mini PI: supervising students, teaching, hosting visitors, keeping the lab running, blah blah. So taking six years to finish makes perfect sense. And the Germans feel no urgency whatsoever; part of those six years is spent taking it easy.

Here, the professor meets the PhD students often, stays very up to date, and knows exactly what everyone is working on and how far they’ve got. Dutch PhD students are much like those in China or the US: more like students. They’re paid a lot more than in either of those places, of course, but a lot less than in Germany (about €1,600 after tax in the first year, without the 30% ruling, a Dutch tax break for employees recruited from abroad). They don’t do much teaching or supervising and can spend most of their time on research.

5. Daily life

The pace of life is similar in both countries; they are close neighbors and both Germanic peoples, after all. But in the Netherlands I have to mention the cycle paths that go everywhere. Is there a Western country I haven’t been to?! And never have I seen a bicycle highway! In the Netherlands the bicycle reigns supreme. Urban planning bends over backwards for cyclists, and the whole world gives way to them. Once, driving, I trailed a cyclist for four or five blocks. The little street had no bike lane, so bikes and cars shared it, and the cyclist, who knew perfectly well I was behind him, just pedaled along at a leisurely pace, paying me no attention whatsoever...
